facts.fact: Even in the Great Depression Coney Island drew millions of visitors, says NYC Parks.
facts.quote: even during the great depression, the promise of fun at coney island continued to draw millions of visitors
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: The July 1932 fire was called the worst in Coney Island's history and consumed 100 feet of boardwalk.
facts.quote: this fire, considered the worst in coney island's history, consumed 100 feet of the boardwalk
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: Thousands fled the burning 1932 bathhouses leaving their clothes behind on the beach.
facts.quote: thousands more were left naked and dripping on the beach after abandoning their clothes as they ran out of the burning bathhouses
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: The 1932 fire is blamed on kids playing with matches.
facts.quote: the cause? kids playing with matches, denson said.
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: At Dreamland's 1911 fire a burning lion ran down Surf Avenue.
facts.quote: a flaming lion ran down surf avenue and climbed the ben-hur ride
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: The 1911 Dreamland blaze began when sparks from popping light bulbs landed on hot tar used to seal the Hellgate ride.
facts.quote: workers were sealing a leak in the hellgate water ride with tar when several of the light bulbs above them popped
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: Dreamland was destroyed by fire in 1911 after surviving only a few years.
facts.quote: dreamland survived until 1911, when it was destroyed in one of the many fires common on coney island during the early 20th century

facts.fact: The Elephantine Colossus burned on 27 September 1896.
facts.quote: when the elephant caught fire on september 27, 1896, it had not been used for several years

facts.fact: Wikipedia lists the Elephantine Colossus at 122 feet tall and seven stories.
facts.quote: at 122 feet (37 m) tall

facts.fact: Brooklyn Public Library calls the elephant twelve stories high with thirty-one rooms.
facts.quote: stood twelve stories high and contained a total of thirty-one rooms
facts.source_title: POTW: The Elephantine Colossus - Brooklyn Public Library

facts.fact: The elephant cost $65,000 to build.
facts.quote: construction was reported to have cost $65,000

facts.fact: Visitors could look through telescopes in the elephant's eyes.
facts.quote: the elephant's eyes contained telescopes and acted as an observatory for visitors

facts.fact: By 1890 the elephant hotel was operating as a brothel.
facts.quote: by 1890, when hard times befell its proprietors - a brothel
facts.source_title: POTW: The Elephantine Colossus - Brooklyn Public Library

facts.fact: The elephant fire is blamed on a forgotten cigar and flames shot from the elephant's eyes.
facts.quote: caught fire after someone forgot to put out his cigar
facts.source_title: A look back on Coney Island's fiery history - Brooklyn Paper

facts.fact: Luna Park lit its lights at 8 p.m. on 16 May 1903 and opened to 45,000 guests.
facts.quote: the park's gates opened five minutes later to a crowd of 45,000 guests

facts.fact: Luna Park admission was ten cents in 1903, with some rides up to 25 cents extra.
facts.quote: admission to the park was ten cents

facts.fact: Luna Park drew 142,000 guests on Independence Day 1903.
facts.quote: recording 142,000 guests on independence day in 1903

facts.fact: Thompson and Dundy spent $700,000 on Luna Park though they advertised a million.
facts.quote: the men spent $700,000 (although they advertised it as $1 million)

facts.fact: Luna Park earned back 90 percent of its construction cost in under three months.
facts.quote: had recovered 90 percent of luna park's construction cost less than three months after its grand opening

facts.fact: Topsy the elephant was killed on the Luna Park site in January 1903.
facts.quote: thompson and dundy ultimately electrocuted topsy, then killed her using cyanide, in january 1903

facts.fact: By the late 1900s Luna Park took five million guests a year.
facts.quote: it accommodated five million guests a year

facts.fact: In the Depression Luna Park could not compete with the free beach.
facts.quote: they were unable to compete with coney island's beach, which charged no admission

facts.fact: Creditors petitioned Luna Park into receivership in 1933.
facts.quote: three of the park's creditors filed a bankruptcy petition against luna park in 1933

facts.fact: During WWII Luna Park had to dim its lights for security.
facts.quote: the park had to keep its lights dimmed for wartime security

facts.fact: A fire on 13 August 1944 destroyed the western half of Luna Park, causing $800,000 in damage.
facts.quote: a fire on august 13, 1944, destroyed much of luna park, causing $800,000 in damage

facts.fact: Luna Park's original attractions included an infant incubator.
facts.quote: the park's original rides and attractions also included an infant incubator

facts.fact: Steeplechase cut staff to 70 in 1945, versus 300 in a normal year, because of the wartime draft.
facts.quote: only 70 people worked at steeplechase that year, compared to 300 in a normal operating year

facts.fact: In 1946 Steeplechase's pool operators used a season-pass scheme that effectively locked out African Americans.
facts.quote: season pass scheme that effectively locked out african americans from using the pool

facts.fact: Steeplechase's Parachute Jump opened in 1941 with 12 parachutes on a 250-foot tower, brought from the 1939 World's Fair.
facts.quote: opened in 1941 and contained 12 parachutes descending from a 250-foot-tall

facts.fact: A September 1939 fire at Steeplechase injured 18 and caused $200,000 in damage.
facts.quote: a conflagration in september 1939 caused $200,000 in damage and injured 18 people

facts.fact: In 1933 fifty-seven people were hurt when an overcrowded Steeplechase balcony collapsed.
facts.quote: in 1933, fifty-seven people were hurt in a balcony collapse caused by overcrowding

facts.fact: By the early 1920s Coney Island parks were calmer, though the beachfront was rundown.
facts.quote: by the early 1920s, the crowds at steeplechase and other coney island parks had become more mellow and orderly

facts.fact: Steeplechase held a grandma's beauty contest from 1932.
facts.quote: grandma's beauty contest, which started in 1932

facts.fact: By 1904 five railroads served Coney Island.
facts.quote: by 1904, there were five railroads to coney island

facts.fact: From about 1880 to World War II, Coney Island was the largest amusement area in the United States.
facts.quote: coney island was the largest amusement area in the united states, attracting several million visitors per year

facts.fact: In the 1890s Norton's Point became the gated community of Sea Gate for the wealthy.
facts.quote: norton's point on the western side of coney island was developed into sea gate, a gated summer community that catered mainly to the wealthy

facts.fact: Couney's 1896 Berlin exhibit kept six premature infants alive for the two-month fair.
facts.quote: couney kept all six infants in incubators in a pavilion at the exposition
facts.source_title: Martin Couney and incubator exhibits from 1896 to 1943 - Embryo Project Encyclopedia (ASU)

facts.fact: Couney charged the public 25 cents to see his Coney Island incubator babies.
facts.quote: the public who came to see couney's exhibit on coney island paid an admission fee of 25 cents
facts.source_title: Martin Couney and incubator exhibits from 1896 to 1943 - Embryo Project Encyclopedia (ASU)

facts.fact: Couney never charged parents; entrance fees paid for the clinic.
facts.quote: couney never charged parents a fee for the care he gave their infants
facts.source_title: Dr. Martin Couney - Coney Island History Project

facts.fact: Couney treated over 8,000 premature infants and over 6,500 lived.
facts.quote: couney treated more than 8,000 premature infants, over 6,500 of whom lived
facts.source_title: Martin Couney and incubator exhibits from 1896 to 1943 - Embryo Project Encyclopedia (ASU)

facts.fact: Historians now believe Couney was not a medical doctor.
facts.quote: though historians now believe he was not a medical doctor
facts.source_title: Baby incubators: from boardwalk sideshow to medical marvel - History.com

facts.fact: Couney ran one exhibit at Luna Park from 1903 to 1943 and another at Dreamland from 1904 until the 1911 fire.
facts.quote: one in luna park from 1903 until 1943, and another in dreamland from 1904 until the fire of 1911
facts.source_title: Dr. Martin Couney - Coney Island History Project

facts.fact: ASU dates Couney's Luna Park exhibit 1904 to 1943.
facts.quote: couney held an exhibit in luna park from 1904 until 1943
facts.source_title: Martin Couney and incubator exhibits from 1896 to 1943 - Embryo Project Encyclopedia (ASU)

facts.fact: Couney employed five wet-nurses to feed the infants.
facts.quote: couney employed five wet-nurses to feed the infants
facts.source_title: Martin Couney and incubator exhibits from 1896 to 1943 - Embryo Project Encyclopedia (ASU)

facts.fact: Lucille Horn, a 1920 incubator baby, said the crowd treated it more like a freak show.
facts.quote: i think it was definitely more of a freak show.
facts.source_title: Baby incubators: from boardwalk sideshow to medical marvel - History.com

facts.fact: Couney died alone at his Sea Gate home in 1950.
facts.quote: couney retired and died alone at his home in sea gate in 1950
facts.source_title: Dr. Martin Couney - Coney Island History Project

facts.fact: The medical establishment did not accept incubators until the 1930s, so Couney had to run his clinic as a sideshow.
facts.quote: it is hard to believe that incubators were not used or accepted by the medical establishment until the 1930s
facts.source_title: Dr. Martin Couney - Coney Island History Project

facts.fact: Charles Feltman began in 1867 pushing a pie wagon through the dunes.
facts.quote: charles feltman began his career in 1867 pushing a pie wagon through the sand dunes of coney island

facts.fact: By the 1920s Feltman's served over five million customers a year and sold 40,000 hot dogs a day.
facts.quote: serving more than five million customers a year and selling 40,000 hot dogs a day

facts.fact: Feltman's Coney Island red hots sold for ten cents each.
facts.quote: sold for ten cents each

facts.fact: Nathan Handwerker sold hot dogs at five cents, half Feltman's price, after opening in 1916 with $300 saved.
facts.quote: which handwerker sold for five cents, half the price of feltman's

facts.fact: A local legend says Nathan hired unemployed men in doctor costumes to eat at his stand.
facts.quote: nathan had just hired unemployed men to put on doctor costumes and eat all day at his stand
facts.source_title: Nathan's Famous - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Feltman's lasted until 1954.
facts.quote: feltman's lasted until 1954

facts.fact: The Switchback Railway, America's first roller coaster, opened 16 June 1884 at Coney Island.
facts.quote: on june 16, 1884, the country's first roller coaster opened at coney island

facts.fact: The Switchback Railway cost a nickel and ran about six miles per hour.
facts.quote: the one-minute-long ride cost only five cents

facts.fact: The Cyclone opened 26 June 1927 for 25 cents a ride.
facts.quote: while it only cost $.25 to ride when it first opened

facts.fact: Coney Island had the first working escalator in 1896.
facts.quote: the coney island installation is said to have carried over 75,000 patrons over its two-week residency

facts.fact: Coney Island's 1920s wooden velodrome seated about 10,000.
facts.quote: the velodrome was a wooden racetrack that seated approximately 10,000 people

facts.fact: New York subway fares were five cents from 1904 to 1948.
facts.quote: the fare for a ride on the subway of any length was 5 cents

facts.fact: An Atlas Obscura line says the subway fare to Coney Island dropped from ten to five cents in 1920, which conflicts with the fare history.
facts.quote: in 1920, the mta lowered the price of a subway ride to coney island from ten cents to five

facts.fact: Fortune said in 1938 the Nickel Empire peaked in the mid-1920s and had declined since.
facts.quote: the nickel empire reached its peak during the middle 1920's

facts.fact: The V&A dates Weegee's Coney Island beach photo to 1940, printed about 1980.
facts.quote: photograph by weegee, 'coney island', gelatin silver print 1940, printed by sid kaplan c.1980
facts.source_title: Coney Island photograph by Weegee - V&A

facts.fact: Weegee shot his crowd picture from an elevated lifeguard station.
facts.quote: shot from an elevated lifeguard station

facts.fact: Weegee photographed Coney Island crowds each summer for the newspaper PM.
facts.quote: for pm, a tabloid-style newspaper for which he did occasional freelance work

facts.fact: Landowners had filled part of Coney Island Creek by 1924.
facts.quote: by 1924 local land owners had filled a portion of the creek

facts.fact: Belt Parkway construction in the 1930s filled more of the creek.
facts.quote: a major section of the creek was further filled in to allow construction of the belt parkway in the 1930s

facts.fact: Fill for the 1962 Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge finished the job, leaving the creek an inlet.
facts.quote: more fill was added in 1962 with the construction of the verrazzano-narrows bridge

facts.fact: A plan existed to turn the creek into the Gravesend ship canal.
facts.quote: there were plans to turn the creek into the gravesend ship canal

facts.fact: Calvert Vaux disappeared on a foggy November morning in 1895 and was found in Gravesend Bay.
facts.quote: on a foggy november morning in 1895
facts.source_title: Coney Island Creek Park history - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: A large section of the creek was filled in the 1920s and 1930s, per Wikipedia, turning the island into a peninsula.
facts.quote: a large section of the creek was filled in the 1920s and 1930s, turning the island into a peninsula
